title: Baijiu Hangover: Why Chinese Liquor Hits Hard and What Helps
excerpt: Why baijiu hangovers are so rough: real alcohol per banquet glass, congeners and shangtou, the Moutai myth, counterfeit methanol risk, and how to get through ganbei toasts.
metaDescription: Why baijiu hangovers hit so hard: 40-60% ABV, banquet toasts, congeners, the Moutai myth, methanol risks, and what actually helps the next morning.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** baijiu hangovers are rough mainly because baijiu is very strong and it's served in a way that makes the total add up fast. Most baijiu is bottled somewhere between about 40% and 60% alcohol, often in the low 50s. That's stronger than typical vodka or whiskey. At a Chinese banquet it comes in small glasses, but those glasses get refilled for toast after toast, and the custom of *ganbei* (literally "dry the cup") means each one gets finished. By the end of a long dinner, many people have drunk the equivalent of half a bottle of whiskey without ever feeling like they had "a drink." Baijiu also carries a lot of flavor compounds from its unusual fermentation, and some of those may add to how bad the next morning feels.

This guide explains what baijiu actually is, how to count what you drank, why it may hit harder than clean spirits, what's true and false about the "good baijiu doesn't give you a headache" saying, how to get through a banquet in better shape, and what to do the next day.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and common-sense guidance for social drinkers. It isn't a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Get medical help right away if** someone who has been drinking is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning; call 911 or your local emergency number (120 in mainland China). **Also get urgent care if** blurred or "snowy" vision, severe stomach pain, or trouble breathing shows up many hours after drinking, especially if the liquor came from an unknown or suspiciously cheap source. Those can be signs of methanol poisoning from counterfeit alcohol, which needs hospital treatment fast. If you flush red when you drink, take regular medication, are pregnant, or have liver disease, talk to your doctor about whether and how much alcohol is safe for you.

## What Baijiu Is (and Why It's Different)

Baijiu (白酒, "white liquor") is China's traditional distilled spirit. It's usually made from sorghum, sometimes blended with rice, wheat, corn, or glutinous rice. It is often described as the most-consumed spirit in the world by volume, almost entirely because of how much is drunk in China.

What sets it apart is how it's fermented. Most Western spirits start with a liquid mash and a controlled yeast strain. Baijiu is typically made by **solid-state fermentation**: steamed grain is mixed with a starter called **qu** (曲), a brick or cake of grain packed with wild molds, yeasts, and bacteria. That damp grain mixture ferments in pits or jars, sometimes for weeks or months, and some styles go through several rounds of fermentation and distillation. The finished spirit is then aged, often in clay jars.

That process produces a spirit unusually rich in flavor compounds, mainly **esters** (fruity, sweet-smelling compounds) and **higher alcohols**, which are also called fusel alcohols. This is why baijiu has such a strong, distinctive smell that people either love or find shocking on the first sip.

### The main aroma styles

Baijiu is grouped by "aroma type." You don't need to memorize them, but knowing the big ones helps you read a menu or a label:

| Style | Chinese name | Typical character | Well-known examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Strong aroma | 浓香 (nongxiang) | Rich, fruity, pineapple-like; the best-selling style | Wuliangye, Luzhou Laojiao, Yanghe |
| Sauce aroma | 酱香 (jiangxiang) | Savory, earthy, soy-sauce-like; long, complex process | Kweichow Moutai, Langjiu |
| Light aroma | 清香 (qingxiang) | Cleaner, drier, more floral | Fenjiu, Erguotou |
| Rice aroma | 米香 (mixiang) | Lighter, sweeter, rice-based | Guilin Sanhua |

Erguotou, the cheap and very common Beijing style, is a light aroma baijiu. Moutai and Wuliangye are the expensive prestige bottles you'll see at business dinners.

## How Much Alcohol Is Actually in Your Baijiu?

This is the part that explains most baijiu hangovers. The numbers below use a US standard drink, which contains 14 grams of pure alcohol (about the amount in a 12 oz beer at 5% or a 1.5 oz shot of 40% liquor). Check your own bottle's ABV, since it varies a lot.

| Amount | At 42% ABV | At 53% ABV |
|---|---|---|
| Small banquet glass (about 15 ml) | about 0.35 standard drinks | about 0.45 standard drinks |
| One ounce (about 30 ml) | about 0.7 standard drinks | about 0.9 standard drinks |
| 100 ml (two *liang*) | about 2.4 standard drinks | about 3 standard drinks |
| Full 500 ml bottle | about 12 standard drinks | about 15 standard drinks |

The banquet glass is the trap. Each pour looks tiny, so nobody counts. But a dinner with a dozen toasts at 53% is roughly five or six standard drinks, and many banquets go well past a dozen toasts. If you also had beer or wine with the meal, add that on top.

A few things make the count harder:

- **Toasts aren't on your schedule.** At a formal dinner, toasts are often initiated by hosts, senior guests, and anyone who wants to honor someone at the table. You can end up drinking at someone else's pace.
- **Refills are automatic.** Hosts and servers top up glasses as a sign of hospitality, so you lose track of how many you've had.
- **The "liang" system.** In China, baijiu is often ordered or discussed in *liang* (两), which is 50 ml (or 50 grams). "I can drink half a jin" means 250 ml, which at 52% is around 7 standard drinks. Hearing quantities in an unfamiliar unit makes it easy to underestimate.
- **It's very strong neat.** Most people drink baijiu straight and at room temperature, with no mixer or ice to slow them down.

## Why Baijiu Hangovers Can Feel So Bad

A hangover is mainly your body's reaction to the total amount of alcohol you drank: poor sleep, dehydration, an irritated stomach, a wave of inflammation, and the build-up of **acetaldehyde**, the toxic first by-product when your liver breaks alcohol down. Baijiu does all of that like any spirit. On top of the volume, a few things are worth knowing.

### 1. The dose is high and fast

High-strength spirit drunk in quick toasts raises blood alcohol quickly. Big peaks and a long night of drinking tend to mean worse sleep and a heavier next morning. This one factor matters more than anything else on this list.

### 2. Lots of congeners, especially higher alcohols

Congeners are the by-products of fermentation that give drinks their flavor and color. Research comparing drinks has found that congener-rich spirits tend to produce somewhat worse hangovers than clean ones at the same blood alcohol. The best-known study, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010 by Rohsenow and colleagues, found that bourbon produced worse hangovers than vodka in a controlled setting. Our [guide to congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) explains this in more detail.

Baijiu wasn't part of that study, but its fermentation tends to leave it rich in esters and higher alcohols. Higher alcohols (such as isoamyl alcohol, isobutanol, and propanol) are the compounds most often blamed in China for the head-pounding feeling called *shangtou* (上头, literally "goes to the head"). Chinese food scientists and distillers have studied how to lower higher-alcohol levels for exactly this reason. The honest summary is that it's plausible congeners make baijiu hangovers a bit worse, but the size of that effect in people hasn't been measured well, and it's much smaller than the effect of simply drinking a lot.

### 3. Mixing drinks and the long banquet

Banquets often pair baijiu with beer, wine, or both, across several hours of eating. Mixing types doesn't cause a hangover by itself; the old "beer before liquor" rules are mostly myth. What mixing does is add volume, and it makes it harder to count.

### 4. Alcohol flush and acetaldehyde

A large share of people of East Asian descent, commonly estimated at around a third, carry a genetic variant called **ALDH2\*2**. It slows the breakdown of acetaldehyde, so it builds up. The visible sign is the red, hot face known as alcohol flush or "Asian glow," often with a racing heart, headache, and nausea. People with this variant tend to feel unwell faster and may have harsher hangovers.

There's also a longer-term issue. Research has linked regular drinking in people with ALDH2 deficiency to a higher risk of esophageal cancer, because acetaldehyde is a carcinogen. If you flush, that redness is useful information. It's a reason to drink less, not something to cover up with antihistamines before a dinner. Our [complete guide to Asian flush](/never-hungover/complete-guide-asian-flush-comprehensive) covers the genetics and the risks.

## "Good Baijiu Doesn't Give You a Headache": True or False?

You'll hear the saying 好酒不上头 ("good liquor doesn't go to your head") at almost any Chinese dinner. It's half true, and the half that's false is the dangerous part.

**What might be true:** better-made baijiu from established distilleries is produced with more careful control of fermentation, distillation cuts, and aging. That can mean lower levels of some of the harsher compounds, including higher alcohols and methanol, compared with poorly made or counterfeit liquor. Cheap, badly made spirits are a reasonable thing to avoid.

**What's false:** expensive baijiu is still 50% or more alcohol, and alcohol is the main cause of a hangover. A bottle of Moutai consumed over an evening will give you a hangover just as surely as a bottle of anything else at the same strength. If anything, people tend to drink more of a prestige bottle, because it feels rude to waste it and because the saying gives them permission.

There's no good evidence that any brand or price tier of baijiu prevents hangovers. Price may slightly improve the odds of a cleaner spirit. It doesn't change the dose.

## A Real Safety Issue: Counterfeit Baijiu and Methanol

Expensive baijiu brands are widely counterfeited, and fake or illegally produced liquor is one of the main sources of methanol poisoning around the world. Methanol is a toxic alcohol that the body turns into formic acid, which can damage the optic nerve and cause blindness, organ failure, or death.

Methanol poisoning doesn't feel like a normal hangover. Signs to take seriously:

- Symptoms that start or get worse **many hours after drinking**, often 12 to 24 hours later
- **Blurred vision, "snowstorm" vision, sensitivity to light, or loss of vision**
- Severe stomach pain, vomiting, and a feeling of being far sicker than the amount you drank should explain
- Fast or labored breathing, confusion, or seizures

If you notice these, especially after liquor from a street vendor, an unlabeled bottle, or a "bargain" premium brand, go to an emergency room and tell them what you drank. Hospitals have effective treatment, but it works best early. Waiting to see if it's "just a hangover" is the mistake. If several people who shared a bottle get sick, treat it as an emergency for all of them.

For everyday safety: buy from reputable stores, be wary of premium brands sold far below their usual price, and check that seals and packaging look intact.

## How to Get Through a Baijiu Banquet in Better Shape

You often can't control the toasts, but you can control more than you might think. These are the habits that make the biggest difference.

1. **Eat before and during.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol is absorbed. Banquet food is plentiful, so use it. Don't drink on an empty stomach before dinner starts.
2. **Know your number before you sit down.** Decide how many toasts you'll actually drink, and count them. Remember that a dozen small glasses at 53% is roughly five to six standard drinks.
3. **Sip instead of draining every glass.** In many settings it's acceptable to take a small sip for routine toasts and save a full *ganbei* for the important ones, such as the host's opening toast. Watching what others at the table do is the best guide.
4. **Keep your glass from being refilled.** A full glass invites more toasts. A glass that's only partly empty, or a hand over the glass, slows the refills.
5. **Use a reason people accept.** Saying you're driving, taking medication, or have a health condition is widely understood. If you flush, that's a genuine medical reason, and many hosts will respect it.
6. **Drink water or tea between toasts.** It won't cancel the alcohol, but it slows your pace and helps with dehydration. Hot tea is normal at most Chinese meals, so it doesn't stand out.
7. **Don't mix in a lot of beer "to cool down."** Switching to beer between baijiu toasts feels like a break, but it adds alcohol.
8. **Stop early in the evening's second act.** Many hangovers are built at the after-dinner round or the karaoke session that follows. That's the easiest point to stop.

If you're traveling for work and don't drink much at home, be especially careful. Your tolerance may be lower than that of the people you're dining with, and you'll be dealing with jet lag and less sleep on top of it.

## What to Do the Morning After a Baijiu Night

There's no cure for a hangover. The only real fix is time, while your body clears the alcohol and its by-products and recovers from a poor night's sleep. These steps can make that time easier:

- **Rehydrate steadily.** Drink water through the morning. If you were sick or sweated a lot, an oral rehydration drink or something with electrolytes can help. Our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) covers what's worth using.
- **Eat something gentle.** Chinese breakfast staples are well suited: rice porridge (congee), noodle soup, or steamed buns with something salty. Warm, brothy, salty food gives you fluid and sodium and is easy on an upset stomach.
- **Rest.** Alcohol wrecks sleep quality even if you slept for hours. A nap, if you can manage one, often helps more than anything else.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** If you need one for a headache, take a single label dose with food. Ibuprofen and aspirin can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already inflamed, and acetaminophen (Tylenol, paracetamol) needs extra caution after heavy drinking. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) explains the liver risks. For a pounding head, our [hangover headache guide](/never-hungover/hangover-headache-fast-relief-methods-2025) lists safer approaches.
- **Skip "hair of the dog."** Another glass of baijiu the next morning only postpones the hangover and adds to the alcohol your body has to clear.
- **Don't drive** until you're sure the alcohol has cleared. After a heavy baijiu night, you can still be over the limit the next morning. Your body only clears roughly one standard drink per hour, and that varies a lot between people.

### Traditional Chinese hangover remedies

In China you'll be offered plenty of hangover fixes. Here's an honest view:

- **Honey water** is a common home remedy. It gives you fluid and a little sugar, which can help you feel better, but there's no good evidence it speeds up alcohol clearance.
- **Strong tea** is a staple. It helps with fluid, and the caffeine may take the edge off grogginess, but caffeine can also irritate your stomach.
- **Sour or fruity drinks** such as plum juice or tomato juice are popular. They add fluid and some sugar and salt.
- **Herbal hangover products** often include *Hovenia dulcis*, the Japanese raisin tree (枳椇, *zhiju*), which has a long history in Chinese and Korean traditional medicine for drinking. It's the plant that DHM was first studied from. More on that below.

## Baijiu vs. Other Asian Spirits

If you're comparing, here's how baijiu stacks up against other drinks you might meet in East Asia:

- **Soju** is usually 16 to 20% alcohol, so a much lower strength than baijiu. Its hangovers come from drinking whole bottles over long nights. See our [soju hangover guide](/never-hungover/soju-hangover).
- **Sake** is brewed, not distilled, and usually around 15% alcohol. It's easy to drink a lot of because it's served warm or chilled in small cups that get refilled. See our [sake hangover guide](/never-hungover/sake-hangover).
- **Shochu** (Japanese) is distilled, usually around 25%, and often diluted with water, hot water, or tea, which slows the pace.
- **Huangjiu** (Chinese yellow wine, such as Shaoxing) is brewed and usually around 14 to 20%.

Baijiu is the strongest of the group by a wide margin. Ounce for ounce, it's roughly three times as strong as soju or sake.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're more likely to have a bad time with baijiu if you:

- **Flush red** when you drink (ALDH2 deficiency)
- Don't drink often, or are drinking with people who drink much more than you
- Are jet-lagged, short on sleep, or traveling for work
- Take medications that interact with alcohol, including sedatives, some antidepressants, blood thinners, diabetes medicines, and certain antibiotics such as metronidazole
- Have liver disease, stomach ulcers, or heart rhythm problems
- Are pregnant or trying to become pregnant

If any of these apply, talk to your doctor before a trip or event where you know baijiu will be served. A short conversation can help you plan what's safe.

## When to See a Doctor

Most baijiu hangovers are miserable but pass within a day. Get medical help if you or someone you're with has:

- Confusion, extreme drowsiness, or can't be woken (possible alcohol poisoning; call emergency services)
- Repeated vomiting, or vomiting blood or material that looks like coffee grounds
- Severe stomach pain that doesn't ease
- Vision problems or breathing trouble many hours after drinking (possible methanol poisoning)
- Chest pain, fainting, or a racing or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest
- Shaking, sweating, anxiety, or seeing things after stopping drinking, if you've been drinking heavily every day for a while. Those can be signs of alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous, so get medical advice rather than waiting it out.

## Where DHM Fits In (Honestly)

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound found in *Hovenia dulcis*, the same raisin tree used in traditional Chinese hangover remedies. Lab and animal studies suggest it may affect how the body handles alcohol and acetaldehyde, and a well-known 2012 study in rats published in the *Journal of Neuroscience* reported that it reduced some effects of alcohol intoxication. That result was in rats, and no trial has tested DHM with high-proof spirits in people.

What DHM won't do is cancel out a dozen glasses of 53% baijiu. There's no good evidence that any supplement prevents a hangover after heavy drinking, and it isn't a reason to drink more or to ignore alcohol flush. If you want to try it alongside sensible drinking, [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simple, low-cost option, and [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) combines DHM with other ingredients. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [guide to preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence.

## The Bottom Line

- Baijiu is usually 40 to 60% alcohol. A full 500 ml bottle at 53% holds about 15 US standard drinks.
- Small banquet glasses and repeated *ganbei* toasts make it easy to drink five, ten, or more standard drinks without noticing.
- Baijiu's fermentation leaves it rich in congeners, which may add somewhat to the hangover, but the amount of alcohol is the main cause.
- Expensive baijiu may be cleaner, but there's no good evidence it prevents hangovers.
- Counterfeit baijiu can contain methanol. Vision problems or severe illness many hours after drinking need emergency care.
- Eat, pace yourself, sip rather than drain routine toasts, drink tea or water between rounds, and stop before the after-party.

For how this drink compares with the rest, see our [ranking of alcohol from least to most hangover](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked).

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does baijiu give such a bad hangover?**

Mostly because of the amount of alcohol. Baijiu is usually 40 to 60% ABV, and at banquets it's drunk in quick toasts that add up fast. A dozen small glasses at 53% is roughly five to six US standard drinks. Baijiu is also rich in congeners, especially higher alcohols, which may make the hangover somewhat worse, and many people flush red when drinking, which tends to make hangovers harsher.

**How strong is baijiu?**

Most baijiu is between about 40% and 60% alcohol, and many popular bottles, including Moutai, are around 53%. Some lower-strength versions are in the 30s. That makes typical baijiu stronger than most vodka, gin, or whiskey, which are usually around 40%. A 500 ml bottle at 53% contains about 15 US standard drinks.

**Does expensive baijiu like Moutai give you less of a hangover?**

There's no good evidence that it does. Well-made baijiu from established distilleries may contain fewer harsh by-products than cheap or counterfeit liquor, which is a fair reason to avoid poorly made spirits. But Moutai is still about 53% alcohol, and alcohol is the main driver of a hangover. People also tend to drink more of a prestige bottle, not less.

**What does "shangtou" mean when people talk about baijiu?**

*Shangtou* (上头) means the liquor "goes to the head": the heavy, pounding feeling some baijiu causes during and after drinking. In China it's often blamed on higher alcohols, also called fusel alcohols, which are by-products of fermentation. That's plausible, but the main cause of feeling bad is still the amount of alcohol you drank.

**How do I refuse baijiu toasts politely?**

Eat well, sip for routine toasts, and save a full drink for the important ones such as the host's first toast. Keeping your glass partly full slows refills. Saying you're driving, taking medication, or have a health reason is widely accepted, and alcohol flush is a genuine medical reason. Watching what others at the table do is the best guide to local etiquette.

**Can baijiu cause methanol poisoning?**

Properly made baijiu from reputable producers is regulated and safe to drink in that respect. The risk comes from counterfeit or illegally made liquor, which can contain dangerous levels of methanol. Warning signs include blurred or "snowy" vision, severe stomach pain, and feeling much sicker than expected, often 12 to 24 hours after drinking. That needs emergency care right away.

**What's the best thing to eat or drink for a baijiu hangover?**

Water, plus something with electrolytes if you were sick, and a gentle, salty, warm breakfast such as congee or noodle soup. Rest helps a lot. Honey water and tea are traditional and can help you feel better, though there's no good evidence they speed up how fast your body clears alcohol. Avoid drinking more alcohol to "fix" it.

**Does DHM help with a baijiu hangover?**

DHM comes from *Hovenia dulcis*, a plant used in traditional Chinese hangover remedies. In rats it eased some signs of intoxication, but there's no good evidence that it prevents a hangover after heavy drinking in people. It won't offset a night of strong baijiu toasts, and it shouldn't be used as a reason to drink more or to ignore alcohol flush.
